steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on MatSAM, which uses the Segment Anything Model to segment microstructures in material micrographs without training. Motivate the problem, cover deep learning and SAM-based prior work, and summarize the method and the main experimental results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why microstructure characterization from micrographs matters; growing data volume
- Limits of DL-based segmentation: annotation cost, weak generalization; pre-training/fine-tuning attempts
- SAM as a visual large model with zero-shot capability; prompt engineering; two kinds of SAM applications
- Our approach: native prompt fails on micrographs -> MatSAM
- Evaluation and main results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Motivation
  - microstructure <-> macro property relationships: central pursuit in materials science
  - micrographs show morphology + spatial distribution of internal structure
  - quantitative characterization -> performance prediction, process optimization
  - automation (material experiment robots, automatic sectioning/grinding machines) + imaging technology -> exponential increase in micrographs
  - processing needs extensive human + computational resources
  - rule-based segmentation enough for simple, well-imaged micrographs
  - DL applied for diverse, densely packed structures under different imaging conditions; algorithms + dedicated software tools
- Limits of DL methods
  - need lots of manual annotation: time-consuming, laborious, needs materials expertise; subjective inconsistencies, wrong labels
  - weak generalizability of task-specific models across materials/microstructures
  - specialist models: hard to apply to new images with varying scales, resolutions, complexities; scaling/cropping make reuse harder
  - pre-training + fine-tuning: robust initial features, then fit target domain
  - prior work: MicroNet (large microscopy dataset), pre-training on material category classification, good out-of-distribution results after transfer learning
  - follow-up: Vision Transformer (ViT), long-range spatial relationships
  - both still need supervised fine-tuning, no practical zero-shot generalizability
- SAM
  - first generalized visual large model (VLM) for promptable segmentation, zero-shot capability
  - largest segmentation dataset (at that time) + large-scale model; billions of image-mask pairs
  - simple architecture + interactive prompt engineering, no extra training (Fig. 1 (a))
  - prompt engineering tailors behavior -> scenario-specific prompts crucial
  - applications: (1) domain-specific datasets + retraining/fine-tuning (annotation-hungry); (2) task-specific prompt engineering (flexible, cheaper)
- MatSAM
  - native point prompt on micrographs (Fig. 1 (b)): fails on most microstructures in crack, phase, grain images
  - cause: SAM's bias toward natural images, native prompts incompatible with microstructures
  - MatSAM (Materials Segment Anything Model): native grid points + structure-aware prompt generation + candidate region screening
  - unsupervised, training-free, universal; imaging-agnostic extraction
- Evaluation
  - vs. conventional and DL-based (supervised) methods, quantitative + qualitative
  - 16 sets of micrographs, public + in-house; optical microscopes (OMs), scanning electron microscopes (SEMs)
  - clearly better than conventional methods, esp. eleven polycrystalline/multiphase datasets: PI-1, PI-2, HEA, DP590-1, DP590-2, etc.
  - on par with / better than supervised methods on PI-1 and SS
  - NBS-3 and UHCS: beats original supervised methods, IoU +3.17% and +4.8%
  - confirms generalizability; first application of visual large model to material micrographs; new research paradigm, faster materials design

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Figuring out the relationships between microstructures and macro properties has been a central pursuit in materials science for a long time. Micrographs, also called microscopy images, give visual insights into the morphology and the spatial distribution of the internal structure of a material. So quantitatively characterizing microstructures is crucial for performance prediction and process optimization. There have been advances in automation, including material experiment robots and automatic sectioning and grinding machines, and in imaging technology, and these have led to an exponential increase in diverse material micrographs. Processing this data often needs a lot of human and computational resources. For simple micrographs that are well imaged, conventional rule-based image segmentation techniques could be enough. To deal with diverse and densely packed structures under different imaging conditions, deep learning (DL) has been applied successfully to material micrograph analysis, and various algorithms and dedicated software tools have appeared.

However, DL-based methods only work if there is a large amount of manually annotated data. Annotating is time-consuming and laborious, and it also needs more expertise in materials science than natural images do. Subjective inconsistencies and wrong labels often happen. Another big problem is that these task-specific models generalize weakly across different materials and microstructures. Specialist models for micrograph segmentation get optimal performance on certain materials and microstructures, and this restricts their use on new images with different scales, resolutions, and complexities. Operations like image scaling and cropping also make it harder to reuse the models. To give the model generalizability, pre-training followed by fine-tuning is used a lot, which is a popular learning paradigm that transfers the learned knowledge to adapt to the downstream task. Pre-training on a large-scale dataset gives models robust initial feature representations. Then fine-tuning with a smaller, task-specific dataset pushes the models to fit the target domain. For segmenting micrographs of materials, prior work developed MicroNet, a large microscopy dataset, and used a pre-training strategy for material category classification. After transfer learning, the pre-trained model got impressive out-of-distribution segmentation results. Building on this, another study used the highly scalable Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to explore the potential of perceiving long-range spatial relationships in microscopy images. But both approaches still need extra supervised fine-tuning, and they cannot really generalize zero-shot in practice when they face unseen material micrographs.

- SAM
  - first generalized visual large model (VLM) for promptable segmentation, zero-shot capability
  - largest segmentation dataset (at that time) + large-scale model, billions of image-mask pairs, simple architecture + interactive prompt engineering (Fig. 1 (a))
  - prompt engineering tailors model behavior -> scenario-specific prompts crucial
  - two kinds of applications: (1) domain-specific datasets + retraining/fine-tuning, annotation-hungry; (2) task-specific prompt engineering, flexible + cheaper
- MatSAM
  - native point prompt fails on most microstructures in crack, phase, grain micrographs (Fig. 1 (b)); SAM biased toward natural images
  - MatSAM (Materials Segment Anything Model): native grid points + structure-aware prompt generation + candidate region screening
  - unsupervised, training-free, universal, imaging-agnostic
- Evaluation
  - vs. conventional + DL-based (supervised) methods; 16 sets of micrographs (public + in-house), OMs and SEMs
  - better than conventional methods, esp. eleven polycrystalline/multiphase datasets (PI-1, PI-2, HEA, DP590-1, DP590-2, etc.)
  - on par with / better than supervised methods on PI-1 and SS
  - NBS-3, UHCS: beats original supervised methods, IoU +3.17% / +4.8%
  - first visual large model applied to material micrographs; new research paradigm

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Figuring out the relationships between microstructures and macro properties has been a central pursuit in materials science for a long time. Micrographs, also called microscopy images, give visual insights into the morphology and the spatial distribution of the internal structure of a material. So quantitatively characterizing microstructures is crucial for performance prediction and process optimization. There have been advances in automation, including material experiment robots and automatic sectioning and grinding machines, and in imaging technology, and these have led to an exponential increase in diverse material micrographs. Processing this data often needs a lot of human and computational resources. For simple micrographs that are well imaged, conventional rule-based image segmentation techniques could be enough. To deal with diverse and densely packed structures under different imaging conditions, deep learning (DL) has been applied successfully to material micrograph analysis, and various algorithms and dedicated software tools have appeared.

However, DL-based methods only work if there is a large amount of manually annotated data. Annotating is time-consuming and laborious, and it also needs more expertise in materials science than natural images do. Subjective inconsistencies and wrong labels often happen. Another big problem is that these task-specific models generalize weakly across different materials and microstructures. Specialist models for micrograph segmentation get optimal performance on certain materials and microstructures, and this restricts their use on new images with different scales, resolutions, and complexities. Operations like image scaling and cropping also make it harder to reuse the models. To give the model generalizability, pre-training followed by fine-tuning is used a lot, which is a popular learning paradigm that transfers the learned knowledge to adapt to the downstream task. Pre-training on a large-scale dataset gives models robust initial feature representations. Then fine-tuning with a smaller, task-specific dataset pushes the models to fit the target domain. For segmenting micrographs of materials, prior work developed MicroNet, a large microscopy dataset, and used a pre-training strategy for material category classification. After transfer learning, the pre-trained model got impressive out-of-distribution segmentation results. Building on this, another study used the highly scalable Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to explore the potential of perceiving long-range spatial relationships in microscopy images. But both approaches still need extra supervised fine-tuning, and they cannot really generalize zero-shot in practice when they face unseen material micrographs.

Segment Anything Model (SAM) was the first generalized visual large model (VLM) for promptable image segmentation, and it brought zero-shot capability. SAM built both the largest segmentation dataset (at that time) and a matching large-scale segmentation model. It was trained on billions of image-mask pairs, and it used a simple architecture design and interactive prompt engineering to segment unseen images accurately without additional training (see Fig. 1 (a)). Prompt engineering tailors how the model behaves through crafted prompts, and this influences its output. So designing prompts for specific scenarios becomes crucial to generalize the VLM to diverse downstream tasks in a cost-effective way. Existing applications of SAM mostly fall into two categories: (1) building a domain-specific dataset and retraining or fine-tuning the model, which is held back by a huge demand for annotations; or (2) designing task-specific prompt engineering, which is more flexible and costs less.

In this work we first explore how versatile SAM is for material micrographs and we assess the native point prompt on diverse microscopy images (see Fig. 1 (b)). The native approach fails to recognize and segment most of the microstructures in three types of micrographs (crack, phase, and grain). This can be attributed to SAM's inherent bias toward natural images, i.e., the native point prompts are incompatible with the characteristics of various microstructures. Material microstructures are complex and diverse, and they need accurate extraction and generalizability for model reuse, so we introduce MatSAM (Materials Segment Anything Model) for segmenting extensive and typical material micrographs. Besides native grid points, MatSAM also uses a structure-aware prompt generation strategy to deliver prompt points adaptively, and then candidate regions are screened to give the final segmentation results. So MatSAM allows unsupervised, training-free, and universal segmentation of microscopy images that characterize typical microstructures of widespread materials, and in the end it achieves accurate and efficient identification and extraction of material microstructures that is imaging-agnostic.

We evaluate how MatSAM performs by comparing its segmentation results with conventional and DL-based (supervised) methods, both quantitatively and qualitatively. The experiments are done on publicly available and in-house datasets of 16 sets of material micrographs. These cover multiple types of microstructures and are imaged with optical microscopes (OMs) and scanning electron microscopes (SEMs). Without manual annotations, MatSAM shows a significant advantage in segmentation accuracy over conventional methods, as expected. The advantage is bigger for micrographs with complex and diverse microstructures, for example the superior performance on eleven datasets of polycrystalline and multiphase materials, including pure iron (PI-1, PI-2), high entropy alloy (HEA), dual-phase steel (DP590-1, DP590-2), etc. Also, without extra training, the accuracies achieved by SAM are on par with or even better than typical supervised learning methods on two polycrystalline images (PI-1 and SS). Surprisingly, on two publicly available datasets that come with test images, nickel-based superalloy (NBS-3) and ultra-high-carbon steel (UHCS), MatSAM outperforms the supervised methods proposed in the original papers, and it improves intersection over union (IoU) by 3.17% and 4.8%, respectively. These results confirm that MatSAM generalizes under zero-shot and training-free conditions. Accurately segmenting unseen images with varying visual features and imaging quality, across different materials, microstructures, and imaging techniques, helps the rapid quantitative characterization of material microstructures. Given how well it extracts microstructures, we believe MatSAM, which is the first application (as far as we know) of a visual large model to analyzing material micrographs, can encourage a new research paradigm in the field and so speed up the design of new materials.

steps.text:
Determining the relationships between microstructures and macro properties has long been a central pursuit in materials science [1,2,3,4]. Micrographs (or microscopy images) provide visual insights into the morphology and spatial distribution of the internal structure of a material [5,6,7]. Quantitatively characterizing microstructures is therefore crucial for performance prediction and process optimization [8]. Advances in automation – including material experiment robots [9] and automatic sectioning and grinding machines [10] – and in imaging technology [11,7] have led to an exponential increase in diverse material micrographs. Processing this data often requires extensive human and computational resources. Conventional rule-based image segmentation techniques can suffice for simple, well-imaged micrographs [12,13,14]. To handle diverse and densely packed structures under different imaging conditions, deep learning (DL) has been successfully applied to material micrograph analysis [5,15,16], and various algorithms [17] and dedicated software tools [18] have emerged.

Unfortunately, the effectiveness of DL-based methods depends on a substantial amount of manually annotated data [19]. The annotation process is not only time-consuming and laborious but also requires more expertise in materials science than for natural images, and subjective inconsistencies and erroneous labels often occur. Another notorious hurdle is the weak generalizability of these task-specific models across different materials and microstructures [20]. Specialist models for micrograph segmentation achieve optimal performance on certain materials and microstructures, which restricts their applicability to new images with varying scales, resolutions, and complexities. Operations like image scaling and cropping further exacerbate the challenge of reusing the models. To give models generalizability, pre-training followed by fine-tuning, a popular learning paradigm that transfers learned knowledge to the downstream task, is extensively used [21]. By pre-training on a large-scale dataset, models acquire robust initial feature representations; subsequent fine-tuning with a smaller, task-specific dataset then pushes them to fit the target domain. For the segmentation of micrographs of materials, [20] developed MicroNet, a large microscopy dataset, and implemented a pre-training strategy for material category classification. After transfer learning, the pre-trained model achieved impressive out-of-distribution segmentation results. Building upon this work, [22] employed the highly scalable Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture [23] to explore the potential of long-range spatial relationship perception in microscopy images. Nonetheless, both approaches still require extra supervised fine-tuning and lack practical zero-shot generalizability when facing unseen material micrographs.

Segment Anything Model (SAM) [24] emerged as the first generalized visual large model (VLM) for promptable image segmentation, bringing with it zero-shot capability [25]. SAM established both the largest segmentation dataset (at that time) and a corresponding large-scale segmentation model. Trained on billions of image-mask pairs, SAM adopted a simple architecture design and interactive prompt engineering to accurately segment unseen images without additional training (see Fig. 1 (a)). Prompt engineering tailors the behavior of the model through crafted prompts, influencing its output [26]. Designing scenario-specific prompts therefore becomes crucial for cost-effectively generalizing the VLM to diverse downstream tasks. Existing applications of SAM largely fall into two categories: (1) constructing a domain-specific dataset [27,28] and retraining or fine-tuning the model [29,30,31,32], which is hindered by a huge demand for annotations; or (2) designing task-specific prompt engineering [33,34], which offers higher flexibility and lower cost.

In this work, we first explore the versatility of SAM for material micrographs and assess the native point prompt on diverse microscopy images (see Fig. 1 (b)). The native approach fails to recognize and segment most microstructures in three types of micrographs (crack, phase, and grain), which can be attributed to SAM's inherent bias toward natural images, i.e., the incompatibility between native point prompts and the characteristics of various microstructures. Given the complexity and diversity of material microstructures, which require accurate extraction and generalizability for model reuse, we introduce MatSAM (Materials Segment Anything Model) for segmenting extensive and typical material micrographs. In addition to native grid points, MatSAM employs a structure-aware prompt generation strategy to adaptively deliver prompt points, followed by candidate region screening to yield the final segmentation results. MatSAM thus enables unsupervised, training-free, and universal segmentation of microscopy images characterizing typical microstructures of widespread materials, and ultimately achieves accurate and efficient identification and extraction of imaging-agnostic material microstructures.

We evaluate the performance of MatSAM by comparing its segmentation results with those of conventional and DL-based (supervised) methods, quantitatively and qualitatively. Experiments are conducted on publicly available and in-house datasets of 16 sets of material micrographs, which encompass multiple types of microstructures and are imaged via optical microscopes (OMs) and scanning electron microscopes (SEMs). As expected, without manual annotations, MatSAM shows a significant advantage in segmentation accuracy over conventional methods. This advantage is particularly pronounced for micrographs with complex and diverse microstructures, as shown by the superior performance on eleven datasets of polycrystalline and multiphase materials, including pure iron (PI-1, PI-2), high entropy alloy (HEA), dual-phase steel (DP590-1, DP590-2), etc. Notably, without any extra training, the accuracies achieved by SAM are on par with, or even surpass, typical supervised learning methods [35,36,37] on two polycrystalline images (PI-1 and SS). Surprisingly, on two publicly available datasets with provided test images (nickel-based superalloy (NBS-3 [20]) and ultra-high-carbon steel (UHCS [38])), MatSAM outperforms the supervised methods proposed in the original papers [20], improving intersection over union (IoU) [39] by 3.17% and 4.8%, respectively. These results confirm the generalizability of MatSAM under zero-shot and training-free conditions. Accurate segmentation of unseen images with varying visual features and imaging quality, across different materials, microstructures, and imaging techniques, facilitates the rapid quantitative characterization of material microstructures. Given its competence in microstructure extraction, we believe MatSAM, to our best knowledge the first application of a visual large model to the analysis of material micrographs, can encourage a new research paradigm in the field and thus accelerate the design of new materials.
